A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by the same authors. Their main texts, figures, equations, references, and Appendices A–B are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original DOTMark noise simulations, comparisons across image classes, and simulated cryo-EM experiments, including results averaged over 100 trials.

after.justification: v3 retains original image-noise and cryo-EM simulation results and adds a spatial-shift-versus-noise experiment in Section 4.3 and Figure 8.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same positive/negative-part construction for signed Wasserstein discrepancies and the same zero-sum Gaussian noise model. The unbalanced-transport extension already appears in v2 Appendix B; the new bounds and experiments do not establish a changed computational method.

E1.justification: DOTMark microscopy images, white-noise images, classic images, sparse synthetic images, and simulated E. coli Hsp90 projections remain covered. The new shift diagnostic analyzes translation and additive noise already represented in v2. The corrected DOTMark description in Section 4.2 agrees with v2 Figure 3's existing caption.

E2.justification: L2, W1, and W2 remain the core evaluated comparators, while W3 remains in the inter-image and sparse-image bound comparisons. The new shift experiment uses the existing core trio; removing theoretical-bound labels from legends does not remove comparators.

E3.justification: v3 Figure 8 introduces a controlled comparison between distances to spatially shifted images, using shifts of 3 and 8 pixels, and distances under increasing Gaussian noise. The original experiments retain their stated image sizes and procedures; their changed displays do not establish that evaluation settings or runs changed.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds a diagnostic testing when additive noise becomes indistinguishable from spatial displacement under each metric. Existing cross-image-class robustness analyses, cryo-EM case studies, and sparse-image explanations of decreasing distance are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 2 newly reports 95% confidence intervals for L2, W1, and W2. Both versions already specify 100 independent trials for this experiment; no increase in runs is stated, and the interval-construction procedure is not explained.

E6.justification: v3 adds shift-versus-noise curves and reports approximately 3.5 times greater noise tolerance for W2 than W1 in that analysis. It replaces the noisy cryo-EM heatmaps, with a visibly more structured L2 pattern, and removes Figure 2's explicit fitted coefficients. These are reporting changes, not established performance gains under matched settings.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.5 and Appendix A add a general-p lower bound, C_p n^(2/p-1) sigma^(1/p), with a new proof. The rescaling theorem drops the nonzero-pixel condition and changes its remainder from O_p(sigma/n) to O_p(1/n). v3 also revises multiscale and Gaussian-variance derivations, tightens the inter-image bound's constant, corrects the squared-L2 expectation, and changes Appendix B's bound and proof to recognize zero total noise mass.

C1.justification: The introduction newly claims this is the first study of Wasserstein noise robustness for measures on a fixed grid and explicitly distinguishes the problem from perturbing point-cloud locations. The central noise-scaling, robustness, and cryo-EM applicability claims otherwise remain.

C2.justification: v3 acknowledges similar W1 and W2 distance rankings under pure additive noise and explains W2's advantage through sensitivity to spatial shifts. Appendix A newly explains the unresolved grid-resolution gap between upper and lower bounds and why minimum-distance arguments miss spatial clustering of noise.

D1.justification: The embedded code link changes from the repository named Quantifying-the-noise-sensitivity-of-wasserstein to Quantifying-wasserstein-noise-sensitivity. A new Reproducibility paragraph specifies code for simulations and all figures. Both versions already advertise code; the PDFs establish changed access instructions, not newly verified availability.

R1.justification: v3 adds Thorpe et al. (2017) on transportation distances for signal analysis and introduces explicit fixed-grid novelty positioning. It also presents unbalanced transport as an extension of the work rather than a largely separate robustness notion. Numerous publication-year and venue updates refer to retained works.

P1.justification: v3 selectively rewrites the abstract and signed-measure explanation, improves grammar, standardizes discrepancy terminology, and adds proof sketches and closing statements. The main sequence of Sections 1–5 and Appendices A–B remains intact, with much of the narrative retained.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column conference layout throughout and extensively reorganizes figure panels, captions, and legends. Image-class plots change from a horizontal strip to a 2-by-2 grid, heatmaps become clean/noisy rows, and Figure 2 displays confidence intervals and lower bounds. The shift experiment adds Figure 8; several other figures are relocated and renumbered.

improvement.justification: For this theory-centered paper, the new lower bound in Theorem 3.5 and Appendix A substantially strengthens the central claim by establishing matching sigma^(1/p) dependence from below, beyond v2's upper bound and empirical support. Corrections to existing derivations further improve mathematical reliability. The grid-resolution gap remains, and v3's structured noisy-L2 heatmap conflicts with its retained random-pattern description, but these limitations do not outweigh the central theoretical gains.
